Infamy is the state of being widely known for something evil, wicked, or deeply shameful. Think of it as the dark twin of fame. Fame means being well-known for something great. Infamy means being well-known for something terrible. It is not just about being bad — it is about being recognized and remembered for that badness. The "known by many people" part is essential to the word.
The Two Senses of the Word

Infamy has two related meanings, and both are used in real life.

The first and more common sense is a state or condition — the status of having a very bad reputation because of something evil or outrageous you did. A villain, a brutal dictator, or a fraudster who ruined thousands of lives might achieve infamy. They are not just bad; they are notorious for their badness, remembered for it across time.

The second sense, slightly rarer, refers to the act itself — an evil, outrageous, or deeply disgraceful action. In this sense, you can speak of "the infamies of a tyrant," meaning the specific wicked deeds they committed. The plural form, infamies, is used this way.

Very strong. Infamy sits at the extreme end of the scale. It is not a mild word for ordinary misconduct or embarrassment. It carries a weight of moral condemnation. When someone achieves infamy, it means history will remember them negatively — they are not just disgraced in private, they are condemned publicly and often permanently. The word signals that the wrongdoing was so significant that it became part of how the world knows that person or event.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words live in the same neighborhood as infamy, but each has a different shade of meaning.

Disgrace means a loss of respect or honor — it focuses on the fall from good standing. A person can be disgraced quietly, even in private. Infamy, by contrast, always involves public awareness. You cannot have infamy in secret.

Notoriety means being famous for something bad or controversial, but it is a softer, more neutral word. A petty criminal might have notoriety. Infamy is stronger — it implies a deeper moral evil, not just a reputation for being troublesome or controversial.

Shame is a personal feeling — you feel shame inside yourself. Infamy is external and public — it is how the world sees you, the reputation that follows you or your name in history.

Dishonor is close in feeling to infamy but typically applies to specific, often personal, violations of a moral or social code — a soldier who betrays his unit is dishonored. Infamy is grander in scale and more permanent in character. It belongs to history books, not just personal relationships.
The Most Famous Use of the Word

The most celebrated use of infamy in modern history comes from U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt's speech to Congress on December 8, 1941, the day after Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor. He called it "a date which will live in infamy." This phrase cemented infamy in the public consciousness as a word for events so shocking and wrong that they are permanently etched into collective memory as a symbol of treachery or evil.
Who or What Can Have Infamy?

A person can achieve infamy — a war criminal, a serial killer, a corrupt leader. A historical event can achieve infamy — a massacre, a betrayal, an atrocity. An act or decision can be called an infamy. Even a place can become infamous — a location where terrible things happened. The word is flexible in what it attaches to, but the requirement is always the same: the subject must be recognized widely for something morally serious and deeply wrong.

Infamy is a formal and serious word. You will encounter it in history, literature, journalism, speeches, and serious writing. It is not a casual, everyday word — you would not use it to describe someone who cut in line or told a bad joke. When you use it, you are signaling that something is not just bad or embarrassing, but genuinely and memorably wicked. It carries a solemn, almost weighty quality.

That said, in informal or humorous contexts, people sometimes use infamy playfully to exaggerate something minor for comic effect — for example, "my terrible cooking has achieved local infamy." This works precisely because the word is so grand and dramatic that applying it to something trivial creates irony. But in serious writing, it should be reserved for genuinely dark subjects.

If you want one clean image to lock this word in your memory: picture a name carved into the wall of history — not in gold, but in warning. That is infamy. It is the kind of fame no one wants, the kind that follows a name long after the person is gone, marking them not for what they built, but for what they destroyed.
